front: What is the core mechanism agentic RAG uses to decide which retrieval strategy to use?
back: A ReAct loop (Reason, Act, Observe, repeat) built on the model's native tool-calling API — the LLM itself decides at runtime which tool to call, rather than code parsing text output.

front: What are the four tools the agentic RAG agent chooses from?
What actually does the "routing" work in this agentic RAG recipe?
back: Just the `description` field on each tool definition — the model reads tool descriptions the same way it reads documentation, with no classifier prompt or hand-written rules involved.

front: How does native tool-calling differ structurally from prompted routing (e.g. `<category>` tags)?
back: Prompted routing has code parse the model's free text after the fact to reconstruct a decision; native tool-calling has the model emit a structured, schema-validated tool_use request as a first-class part of the API response.

front: Why does an agentic RAG loop need a hard iteration cap?
back: A misinterpreted tool result can send the loop down an unproductive path indefinitely, since an open-ended loop has no built-in reason to stop — the cap forces an honest "ran out of budget" exit.

front: Which tool did the agent pick for "What connects label smoothing to the BLEU score improvements?", and why?
back: graph_local_search — the specific, two-entity relational question matched the tool built for exactly that, over the more expensive global search or a plain vector lookup.

front: What real costs does agentic RAG have that a fixed pipeline doesn't?
back: Unpredictable per-query latency/cost (the number of tool calls varies), error compounding from misread results, and harder evaluation since the agent's path itself varies per question.

front: When should you skip agentic RAG in favor of a fixed pipeline?
back: For high-volume, well-understood query patterns (simple FAQ lookups, single-document Q&A) where the right retrieval strategy is already knowable in advance.
